data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on his own terms not as an inductive inference of future success, but as a non-inductive methodological rule aligned with the aim of science (truth), provided one accepts the cost of abandoning any guarantee that this preference yields practical success in novel domains.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the agent's aim shifts from 'finding truth' to 'maximizing predictive success in novel domains,' the Popperian preference loses its rational force without an inductive bridge.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the Tich\u00fd-Miller refutation of verisimilitude holds strictly, then we cannot rationally claim the better-corroborated theory is 'closer to truth,' undermining the link between corroboration and the aim of truth.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the stability of test conditions in the future cannot be assumed even as a methodological decision, the relevance of past corroboration to present choice evaporates.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism distinguishes between 'logical justification' (which requires induction and is rejected) and 'rational preference' (which is volitional and aim-relative). By defining the aim of science as finding true theories, preferring the theory that has best withstood falsification attempts becomes the only rational strategy to pursue that aim, even if we cannot know it will succeed. This avoids smuggling in induction because it makes no claim about the probability of the theory being true or working in the future; it merely states that if truth is the goal, the unrefuted theory is the best available candidate.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
